clue.text: These involve taking leak in different pubs?

definitions.text: These involve taking leak in different pubs?

indicators.note: PUBS made different is its letters rearranged

parts.note: first letter of the rearranged PUBS (BUPS)
the rest of the rearranged PUBS

explanation.surface: A night out spent visiting the gents of every pub on the street.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a booze-up does involve a leak in several pubs. The OOZE goes inside PUBS rearranged as BUPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A booze-up is a drinking session, often a pub crawl, which reliably involves repeated trips to the toilet.

clue.text: (& 22dn.) Two masters who can no longer score, being pissed

definitions.text: Two masters who can no longer score
definitions.meaning: two dead composers, who can no longer write a score
rhyming slang: two composers' names stand in for the word they rhyme with

explanation.surface: Two old men past it in the bedroom, blaming the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: "Score" pretends to mean sexual success; here it is musical notation, since both composers are long dead. Brahms and Liszt is British rhyming slang for drunk, because Liszt rhymes with pissed.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang takes the phrase Brahms and Liszt to stand for pissed, meaning drunk.

clue.text: Where beer belly's found to extend into another's space

definitions.meaning: a beer belly hangs OVER (the) LAP
to spill across into a neighbour's area, as tiles or seats do

explanation.surface: A drinker's paunch spreading onto the next seat.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads the answer as two words, OVER LAP, which is exactly where a gut hangs.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that overlap extend into each other's space.

clue.text: Booze finally gets Mark to act with feeling

indicators.note: take the final letter of Booze

parts.note: a mote is a speck, a tiny mark

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark who can only perform properly after a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a man's name at the start of the sentence; it is the common noun, a speck.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually for an actor overplaying: emoting is performing emotion rather than feeling it.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Was responsible for a leak, like a recent leader of Tories getting hammered

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter of Tories

explanation.surface: A former Conservative leader drunk and responsible for a press leak.
explanation.walkthrough: "Recent leader of Tories" reads as a former party boss; split it into recent = NEW and the leader of Tories = T. "Pissed as a newt" is British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Pissed as a newt is a British idiom for extremely drunk, which is what hammered means.

clue.text: Farage's initial dare to change name

indicators.note: DARE changes the order of its letters
the initial is the first letter of Farage

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage daring someone to change his name, or perhaps his party's.
explanation.walkthrough: Only DARE is rearranged; F stays at the front, as "initial" suggests. Farage is a British right-wing politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Freda is a woman's first name, and crosswords often use a bare "name" for any such given name.

clue.text: Female with one ball, right? Sexy performer

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A saucy cabaret act about a woman with one ball.
explanation.walkthrough: "Ball" wants to be a round object; it is the dance, the Cinderella sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan dancer performs nude or nearly so, hiding behind large feather fans.

clue.text: Within this, you'll hear of an organ placed over a serving of whisky?

parts.note: a shot is a single measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A body part perched above a glass of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: within earshot is the range where you can hear something.
explanation.definitionFit: Earshot is the distance within which sounds can be heard.

clue.text: Forward half of non-drinkers: "Beer's topping!"

indicators.note: AA has two letters; half of it is one A

parts.note: non-drinkers = AA, Alcoholics Anonymous; half is A
the foam on top of a beer

explanation.surface: Teetotallers giving a toast to the frothy top on a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: "Forward" looks like it describes the non-drinkers; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for onward in space or time: pressing forward and pressing on in front are the same movement.

clue.text: Wife's out of stingers — just one did for Cleo

definitions.note: the definition describes one asp; the answer is plural, matching stingers

indicators.note: 'out of' in the sense of having run out

explanation.surface: A wife who has run out of stingers, noting that it took only one to kill Cleopatra.
explanation.walkthrough: Cleo is Cleopatra, who by legend died from the bite of an asp.
explanation.definitionFit: Asps are snakes; one of them killed Cleopatra.

clue.text: Bitter retailers snapped: "EU asshole!"

indicators.note: the letters are broken and put back together

explanation.surface: Angry shopkeepers shouting abuse at a Brussels official.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is the beer, not a mood; "Bitter retailers" are places that sell ale.
explanation.definitionFit: An alehouse is a pub, a retailer of bitter and other beers.

clue.text: Cigar butt evident in wine's aroma gets past tongue

indicators.note: a butt is the end of a cigar, so its last letter

parts.note: a wine's nose is its smell

indicators.note: something evident in a thing can be seen within it

explanation.surface: A wine taster complaining of cigar ash in the bouquet.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tongue" is a language, not the taster's organ; Old Norse is no longer spoken, so past.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse is the language of medieval Scandinavia, a tongue of the past.

clue.text: Whisky? See pissed islanders

definitions.note: Maltese is used as a plural noun here, the people of Malta

indicators.note: pissed means drunk, and a drunk word staggers so its letters fall out of order

explanation.surface: Someone offering whisky and pointing out some drunk islanders.
explanation.walkthrough: "See" looks like an instruction to look; it is only three letters to rearrange. Malta is the Mediterranean island nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maltese are the people of the island of Malta.

clue.text: Loaded pulped

explanation.walkthrough: "Loaded" could be rich; in this drink-themed puzzle it means drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Smashed means both very drunk and crushed to pulp.

clue.text: Crappy Parmesan has Dutch character

indicators.note: PARMESAN is in poor shape, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A cheese snob sneering at poor Parmesan with a Dutch flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: "Character" suggests flavour or personality; it is a printed symbol, the &.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the & symbol is one of the typographic characters, alongside letters, digits and punctuation.

clue.text: Science responsible for half-cut dairy logo

indicators.note: half-cut means drunk, so the letters stagger about

explanation.surface: A lab blamed for a cow on a milk carton being cut in half.
explanation.walkthrough: "Half-cut" looks like trimming the logo; it is slang for drunk, which scrambles every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Radiology is the medical science of imaging with X-rays and similar.

clue.text: Difficulty getting the words out in Gladys' PH, as I articulated

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words

explanation.surface: Someone struggling to pronounce Gladys's PH, perhaps after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The oddly spelt PH is a giveaway that letters are being planted.
explanation.definitionFit: Dysphasia is a disorder of language, typically trouble producing speech.

clue.text: Hack, being tumescent, is distressed

explanation.surface: A journalist upset about his own arousal.
explanation.walkthrough: "Hack" looks like a journalist; it is the verb. Cut up is British slang for upset.
explanation.definitionFit: To be cut up about something is to be very upset by it.

clue.text: Drunk, the recipient of first aid treatment?

definitions.text: the recipient of first aid treatment?
definitions.meaning: given a plaster, a sticking bandage

explanation.surface: A drunk who falls over and ends up bandaged.
explanation.walkthrough: A plaster is the British word for a sticking bandage, so someone patched up has been plastered.
explanation.definitionFit: Plastered means very drunk, and literally means covered with a plaster.

clue.text: On a trip, act pissed, lacking energy

parts.note: E = energy, removed from PEED to leave PED

explanation.surface: A tourist behaving drunkenly and flagging on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pissed" means drunk everywhere else in this puzzle; here it is the other sense, urinated. "On a trip" is hallucinating, not travelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Drug slang: a trip is a hallucinogenic experience, so someone on one has been given drugs.

clue.text: Incapable, this organ, when sheathed in black and white

parts.note: the organ the answer itself names

explanation.surface: An organ too useless to work, wrapped in a black and white covering.
explanation.walkthrough: "Incapable" means drunk here, as in drunk and incapable. "This organ" points at the organ in the answer, the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Pie-eyed is slang for very drunk, too drunk to function.

clue.text: At heart, "boozer" popularly represents this country

indicators.note: the heart of boozer is its middle letters

parts.note: popularly = in informal speech, where Oz is a nickname for a country

explanation.surface: A national stereotype: the drinker as a nation's mascot.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay yields only OZ; you must know Oz is the everyday nickname for Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: "This country" points back at the nickname just produced: Oz is informal slang for the Australian nation.

clue.text: Places army officer back on alcoholic drinks

indicators.note: sending the officer back means reading him from the far end

explanation.surface: A colonel returning to the bar for more drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: "Places" looks like a verb (sets down); it is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a locale is a particular place or setting where something happens.

clue.text: Whopper has feathers stuck on? Don't stand for that

definitions.note: the definition describes a lie-down as something you don't stand for

parts.note: a whopper is a big lie

explanation.surface: Someone refusing to put up with a tall tale that has been dressed up with feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: "Don't stand for that" sounds like refusing to tolerate something; read literally, during a lie-down you are not standing.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-down is a rest taken lying flat, not standing.

clue.text: (see 1 dn.)
(see 4dn.)
Legless batsman's partial stroke

definitions.meaning: HALF a CUT, a cricket stroke

explanation.surface: A cricketer too drunk to finish his shot.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a cut is a stroke played square on the off side. "Legless" is slang for drunk, and "leg" is also a cricket term, which strengthens the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-cut and legless are both British slang for drunk.

clue.text: Creepy thing in Mali (an alcoholic)

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words

explanation.surface: A sinister figure in Mali who drinks too much.
explanation.walkthrough: "Creepy" means creeping, as a climbing plant creeps, not sinister.
explanation.definitionFit: A liana is a woody climbing vine that creeps up trees.

clue.text: For example, drunkard has no time for authority

indicators.note: the drunkard has no time, so the letter for time is missing from him

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
T = time, removed from SOT to leave SO

explanation.walkthrough: "Has no time for" reads as contempt for authority; it is an instruction to drop T. A sot is an old word for a habitual drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: acting on someone's say-so means acting on their word, their authority to decide.

clue.text: Eye welcomes attack on Starmer, finally — "Raver!"

indicators.note: a host who welcomes a guest takes them inside

parts.note: Private Eye, as a magazine, speaks of itself as WE

indicators.note: take the last letter of Starmer

explanation.walkthrough: Eye is the magazine this puzzle appears in, and a magazine refers to itself editorially as "we". W(ASSAIL)E, then R.
explanation.definitionFit: A wassailer is someone out carousing and drinking, a reveller or raver.

clue.text: Two Democrats, covered in trifle, drink

indicators.note: something covered in a coating sits inside it

explanation.surface: Two American politicians smeared in custard dessert, grabbing a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: "Trifle" looks like the British layered pudding; it is the verb, to toy.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddy is a hot drink of spirits, water, sugar and spices.

clue.text: Tight bottomed contrary sailor comes first

indicators.note: a contrary sailor goes the opposite way to everyone else, so his letters run backwards

explanation.surface: A mean, stubborn sailor with a notable backside pushing to the front.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tight" suggests stingy; it is slang for drunk. Rat-arsed is crude British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Rat-arsed and tight both mean drunk.
